Corroboration: จรูญ บุญพันธ์ [Bunphan, Jaroon]. 2525 [1982]. วิธีการทำเป็นการีตในภาษาญัฮกุร (Causativization in Nyah Kur). MA thesis, Chulalongkorn University, ch. 2 sec. 2.2.2, p. 8.
catalog_locator: MKS 16-17 p.56 (page re-rendered and read directly on verification), sec. 1.3.3 'Syllable Structure' under 1.3 'Nyah Kur of Ban Wang Ai Pho'; register/pitch remarks p.51, sec. 1.3.2 Vowels, note 2. Parallel Burmese Mon statement p.39 sec. 1.1.3. Bunphan 1982 ch. 2 p.8 (verified against the source).
catalog_quote: The syllable structure of Nyah Kur words is rendered extremely complex by extensive Thai loans, resulting in such word shapes as CCCVCV́VC (/phyəyáam/ 'to try') and CV́CCVCCV́C (/sókkəprók/ 'dirty'). If we confine ourselves to native Nyah Kur words, they may be either 1) monosyllabic of shape C(C)(C)(C)(C){V́C / V́V(C)} (as illustrated in 1.3.1.1.), implying that a final /C/ is obligatory after short vowels but optional after long vowels and diphthongs; or 2) disyllabic, consisting of an unstressed presyllable of shape /CV-/, where /V/ is always /ə/, plus a stressed syllable having one of the shapes represented in 1) above.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (image-only, 54 pp = MKS 16-17 pp.31-84). I rendered PDF page 26 (= journal p.56) and read it directly: section '1.3.3. Syllable Structure' contains the quoted passage word for word ('The syllable structure of Nyah Kur words is rendered extremely complex by extensive Thai loans, resulting in such word shapes as CCCVCV́VC (/phyəyáam/ 'to try') and CV́CCVCCV́C (/sókkəprók/ 'dirty'). If we confine ourselves to native Nyah Kur words, they may be either 1) monosyllabic of shape C(C)(C)(C)(C){V́C | V́V(C)}.. or 2) disyllabic, consisting of an unstressed presyllable of shape /CV-/, where /V/ is always /ə/, plus a stressed syllable having one of the shapes represented in 1) above.').…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Native Nyah Kur words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in disyllables the initial presyllable /Cə-/ is unstressed and the final (main) syllable carries the stress, i.e. word stress is fixed on the final syllable. Confirmed independently by Bunphan 1982 (Chulalongkorn MA, p.8, Thai): 'ส่วนพยางค์รองประกอบด้วยพยัญชนะเดี่ยวและสระลดรูป /ə/ ทั้งนี้เนื่องจากพยางค์รองเป็นพยางค์ที่ไม่ได้รับการลงเสียงหนัก (unstressed syllable) ฉะนั้นในการบันทึกลักษณะน้ำเสียงจะใส่เครื่องหมายแสดงลักษณะน้ำเสียงเฉพาะพยางค์หลักเท่านั้น' [the minor syllable consists of a single consonant and the reduced vowel /ə/; since the minor syllable is a syllable that does not receive stress (unstressed syllable), register is marked only on the major syllable], file.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said. Polysyllabic Thai loans (e.g. /sókkəprók/) carry Huffman's acute mark on each full syllable, but he does not discuss secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Thai loanwords produce longer word shapes with more than one full syllable and may retain Thai tones (pp.51-52, 56); the fixed: final syllable statement is made for native vocabulary. Nyah Kur is a register (clear vs breathy) language; pitch differences accompany register but are described as non-contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word in citation form (elicited 900-word vocabulary from one speaker, Ban Wang Ai Pho, Amphoe Bamnet Narong, Chaiyaphum, 1970-71). Stress is described via word/syllable structure (presyllable vs main syllable), not phrase prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Huffman 1990 describes Nyah Kur of Ban Wang Ai Pho, Amphoe Bamnet Narong, Chaiyaphum Province (the central/southern dialect group in L-Thongkum's classification); Bunphan 1982 draws on L-Thongkum's dictionary data (Chaiyaphum/Nakhon Ratchasima southern group). Both fall under glottocode nyah1250 (language-level); the northern Phetchabun dialect is not covered by the quoted statement.

tone_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel (1983). Essai de phonétique historique du môn. Mon-Khmer Studies 12. pp. 1-90.
tone_statements.quote: Registres. 1er registre: normal (non marqué); 2nd registre: bas-soufflé (accent grave). [...] Dans l'opposition de registre, le premier est caractérisé par une voix claire sur un ton moyen et le second par une voix soufflée sur un ton plus bas légèrement descendant. Dans les effets expressifs la voix se maintient mieux que le ton. [...] A Ban Ay Pho la différence de ton n'est pas sensible mais la qualité soufflée est très marquée à tel point qu'il est souvent difficile à l'oreille de séparer l'aspiration de la consonne du souffle de la voyelle. En fait ces caractéristiques sont tout autant personnelles que dialectales.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 20-21 (chapter XI 'Présentation sommaire du nyah kur')
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: First-hand auditory field description (no instruments). Confirms the Nyah Kur catalog tone field (register language, pitch a non-contrastive concomitant): register 1 clear voice on mid pitch, register 2 breathy on lower slightly falling pitch, voice quality more stable than pitch, pitch difference not perceptible at Ban Ay Pho. Silent on word stress.

sources.note: p.56 sec. 1.3.3 (Nyah Kur of Ban Wang Ai Pho, Chaiyaphum): native words are either monosyllables or disyllables consisting of an unstressed presyllable /Cə-/ plus a stressed (main, final) syllable; Thai loans add more complex shapes. Also notes register (clear vs breathy) with non-contrastive pitch, and Thai loans retaining tones (pp.51-52).

sources.note: ch.2 p.8 sec. 2.2.2 (Thai, read from page scan): disyllables = minor syllable (single C + reduced /ə/) + major syllable; the minor syllable 'is a syllable that does not receive stress (unstressed syllable)', so register is marked only on the major syllable; e.g. /kətʰàp/. Phonology summary based on Theraphan L-Thongkum's dictionary.
